bridge_result.text: At Q, solar radiation gives the spacecraft an acceleration of 3.2 × 10⁻⁶ m s⁻².
bridge_result.origin: Earlier result supplied so you can start with this topic.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Two particles have the same charge and different masses. After acceleration, they have equal kinetic energies. Compare their de Broglie wavelengths. You may use p = √(2mEₖ).

answer.text: Their wavelengths differ: λ = h/√(2mEₖ), so the more massive particle has the shorter wavelength.

ibd-4367e58fe64b74a3-q10:a.hint: Connect the particle’s wavelength to its momentum, rather than treating it as a photon.
notes: The de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/p. For a non-relativistic particle, p = mv or √(2mE_k).

If accelerated from rest through a voltage magnitude V, E_k = |q|V. Use this only in the non-relativistic regime; E = hc/λ is a photon relation, not a general massive-particle kinetic-energy equation.

ibd-4367e58fe64b74a3-q10:b.i.hint: Consider the change in each photon’s momentum at the surface, then multiply by the arrival rate.
notes: At normal incidence, absorption transfers momentum E/c per photon, while reflection straight back transfers 2E/c. Force is the rate of momentum transfer.
Radiation pressure is I/c for absorption and 2I/c for perfect reflection. For a solar sail, changing distance from the Sun changes incident intensity and hence acceleration.
For “show that”, start from the supplied data and display the intermediate steps. Do not substitute the result you are asked to show as an assumption.

notes: Ignoring drag, horizontal velocity is constant and vertical acceleration is −g when up is positive. Resolve the launch velocity using the angle shown.
At the highest point only the vertical velocity is zero. Use the actual launch and landing heights; the equal-height range formula does not apply to unequal heights.

ibd-4367e58fe64b74a3-q10:d.i.hint: For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the inward acceleration. Use the radius measured from the central body’s centre.
notes: Equating GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), then T = 2πr/v. This leads to T² proportional to r³.
Orbiting objects are in free fall, not outside gravity. A geostationary orbit must also be equatorial, prograde and have Earth’s rotation period.

ibd-59d51577e3fd9550-q34:whole.hint: Consider the energy carried by one photon and the energy needed to release one electron.
notes: Einstein’s photoelectric equation is hf = φ + E_k,max. At threshold, hf₀ = φ; a stopping potential gives E_k,max = eV_stop.

Above threshold, intensity mainly changes the number of emitted electrons; frequency changes the maximum kinetic energy. Below threshold, greater intensity cannot compensate for insufficient photon energy.

ibd-641ca00f2c84853d-q34:whole.hint: Distinguish energy per photon from the rate at which photons arrive.
notes: A photon has E = hf = hc/λ and momentum p = E/c = h/λ. Beam power is photon arrival rate multiplied by energy per photon.
Intensity is power per area. Changing wavelength changes the energy of each photon; changing the number arriving changes the photon rate, so account for both.

ibd-641ca00f2c84853d-q35:whole.hint: Apply both energy and momentum conservation to the photon–electron interaction.
notes: For an initially stationary electron, the Compton wavelength shift is Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos θ), where θ is the photon scattering angle.
The outgoing photon energy is hc/λ′; the electron gains the difference from the incoming photon energy. The photon and electron scattering angles are not the same angle.

If accelerated from rest through a voltage magnitude V, E_k = |q|V. Use this only in the non-relativistic regime; E = hc/λ is a photon relation, not a general massive-particle kinetic-energy equation.

fep-467906ca0a9e425d-q35:whole.hint: Consider the energy carried by one photon and the energy needed to release one electron.
notes: Einstein’s photoelectric equation is hf = φ + E_k,max. At threshold, hf₀ = φ; a stopping potential gives E_k,max = eV_stop.

Above threshold, intensity mainly changes the number of emitted electrons; frequency changes the maximum kinetic energy. Below threshold, greater intensity cannot compensate for insufficient photon energy.

fep-93b29888017e294e-q37:whole.hint: Distinguish energy per photon from the rate at which photons arrive.
notes: A photon has E = hf = hc/λ and momentum p = E/c = h/λ. Beam power is photon arrival rate multiplied by energy per photon.
Intensity is power per area. Changing wavelength changes the energy of each photon; changing the number arriving changes the photon rate, so account for both.
